turns.doctor_question: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Well, I came in because... I just can’t seem to stop launching projects. Work plans, new certification schedules for my team, upgrading the entire home network... actually, I decided to rip out all the old ethernet cables at my house last Tuesday because Cat5e just doesn't cut it anymore if you want true gigabit speeds across a mesh system. I found this incredible bulk deal online for Cat6a, which is really what you need for future-proofing if you're running a lot of smart devices. 

But anyway, I've also been sending out all these messages to old contacts, people I haven't talked to since I got my bachelor's. My buddy Dave from my undergrad actually replied, he's living in Denver now, doing something with solar panels. Great guy, we used to play intramural softball. But yeah, the project stuff just gets so intense that I completely blow past normal limits. I just keep going and going until my wife or my director at work literally has to step in and tell me to put the brakes on.

turns.patient_response:
Yeah, actually... there have been several stretches where everything is just calm, you know? Flat. Like, for a few weeks at a time, I wouldn't be especially up, wouldn't be depressed, just... normal baseline. But I'd still get those things happening. Like, I'd still hear those brief comments when no one was in the room, and I'd look at people's Microsoft Teams statuses and just know they were coded warnings meant for me. 

Which, honestly, Teams is a nightmare anyway. Getting people to actually use their statuses correctly is impossible. They just leave it on 'Away' for three days or they don't sync it with their Outlook calendar. When we did the big migration to Microsoft 365 last year, I had to run a whole training seminar on it. The backend of that migration was brutal, mostly because of the legacy SharePoint sites we had to move over. I ended up writing this massive PowerShell script to map all the old user permissions to the new Azure Active Directory groups. PowerShell is amazing, but you have to be so careful. One wrong command and you can wipe out an entire directory tree. That's why you always, always have to follow the 3-2-1 backup rule. Three copies of your data, two different media types, one offsite. 

I actually built a custom NAS—Network Attached Storage—at home using TrueNAS just to ensure my personal files are safe. I set it up in a RAID Z2 array, which means it can survive two complete hard drive failures at the exact same time without losing a single byte of data. Mechanical drives fail constantly, usually the read/write heads just crash onto the platters, especially if there's a vibration issue in the server chassis. You really have to invest in drives specifically rated for NAS environments, like the WD Reds, because they have vibration tolerance built into the firmware... 

But yeah, even when my mood was totally normal, I'd still see the warnings in the statuses and hear the comments.
